instagram:
1920: The New York Times told its readers a rocket could never work in the vacuum of space, and mocked the physics professor who said it could.

Rockets were fireworks then, tubes of powder that wasted over 98 per cent of their energy. Robert Goddard, a physics professor at Clark University, wanted to reach space. Fireworks burned powder. He burned gasoline and liquid oxygen. His first attempt, on 8 March 1926, failed.

On 16 March 1926, on his aunt Effie Ward's farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, the motor burned for 20 seconds before the rocket lifted. It flew for 2.5 seconds, climbed 12.5 metres and landed 56 metres away in a cabbage patch. 43 years later, liquid fuel rockets flew 3 men to the Moon, and The Times printed a correction: "The Times regrets the error." Last year there were 324 launches to orbit, carrying the satellites behind your maps and weather forecasts.

Builders wanted. The Ad Astra Fellowship: 12 months, a room, food, the labs, the machine shop and the compute at $0, a company in your name from day 1. 1 written application, no credentials needed. Apply at joinadastra.com

Sources: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (heights converted to metres), National Air and Space Museum, Smithsonian Institution Archives, American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, SpaceNews.
